title: A traversal filter that only blocks "../" misses "..\\" — and you can test the miss without touching Windows
assumption: Checking a filename for the substring "../" catches every directory-traversal attempt.

input.description: A filename accepted by a web form where the server later resolves the path on Windows, or a ZIP/tar entry name that uses backslashes.

what_goes_wrong: A blocklist written against the forward-slash form lets the backslash form straight through, and ntpath/path.win32 — which treat backslash as the canonical separator — walk back out of the intended directory exactly as the forward-slash form would.
why: ntpath and path.win32 are pure-path implementations of Windows' own path rules, where backslash is the primary separator even though forward slash also works. A traversal check written only against the string "../" is really checking for a POSIX idiom and has nothing to say about "..\\", so on any code path that eventually resolves the string as a Windows path, the backslash form reaches the same `..` component and climbs out of the base directory just the same.
affects: windows path resolution (backslash is the canonical separator)
ntpath (runs on any host, not just windows)
path.win32 (runs on any host, not just windows)

repros.code:
import ntpath
raw = "..\\..\\windows\\system32"
print("contains ../ :", "../" in raw)
joined = ntpath.join("C:\\srv\\uploads", raw)
print("joined:", joined)
print("normalized:", ntpath.normpath(joined))
repros.expected_output:
contains ../ : False
joined: C:\srv\uploads\..\..\windows\system32
normalized: C:\windows\system32

fix: Normalize with the platform-appropriate path module and compare the RESULT against the resolved base directory; never pattern-match the raw string for one separator style.

test_cases.note: A traversal filter tested only against forward slashes should also be tested against this backslash form before you trust it.
